q.context: A 2.0 kg block rests on a 3.0 kg cart. A horizontal force pulls the cart on a level floor. The floor exerts a constant 5.0 N opposing motion. The block–cart static friction coefficient is 0.25. Use g=10 m/s²; ignore wheel rotation.
q.find: Find the largest pulling force that lets the block remain at rest relative to the cart.
q.prompt: Find the largest pulling force that lets the block remain at rest relative to the cart.
q.hint: Draw the upper block and the whole system separately.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. At this force the upper block needs 5 N, exactly its friction limit; the floor force remains external.
q.feedback_incorrect: Using the full system weight to find upper-contact friction overestimates the limit.
q.explanation: The upper block is accelerated only by static friction, so its acceleration cannot exceed μg=2.5 m/s². For the two bodies together, the internal contact force cancels: F−5=(2+3)a. At the limiting shared acceleration, F=5+5(2.5)=17.5 N.

q.given: A 50.0 kg passenger stands on a scale reading 400 N while the lift moves downwards at 6.00 m/s. The acceleration is constant for the next 2.00 s. Use g=10.0 m/s².
q.prompt: Find the downward distance travelled in those 2.00 s.
q.find: Find the downward distance travelled in those 2.00 s.
q.hint: A scale reads the normal contact force, not mg.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. 400 N<500 N weight gives downward acceleration as specified by the signs.
q.feedback_incorrect: Downward motion alone would not determine acceleration; use the scale reading.
q.explanation: The passenger’s force imbalance determines lift acceleration before motion is calculated. With downward positive, mg−N=ma gives a=(500−400)/50.0=2.00 m/s² downwards. q.context: A 750 kg car climbs a 5.0° hill at a steady 20 m/s. Air and rolling resistance total 450 N. Use g = 10 m/s².
q.prompt: Find the mechanical power delivered by the engine, in kW.
q.hint: Balance drive against slope weight and resistance at steady speed.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Drive force about 1104 N at 20 m/s needs about 22.1 kW.
q.feedback_incorrect: Zero acceleration does not imply zero mechanical power.
q.explanation: Steady speed has zero net slope force but requires positive engine work. The driving force is 450+750(10)sin5°=1104 N. Power Fv=1104(20)=22.1 kW.

q.context: Two satellites have circular orbits around the same planet. B has twice the orbital period of A. Neglect satellite masses and atmospheric drag.
q.given: Two satellites have circular orbits around the same planet. B has twice the orbital period of A. Neglect satellite masses and atmospheric drag.
q.prompt: Find the ratio r_B/r_A.
q.find: Find the ratio r_B/r_A.
q.hint: Combine gravitational circular motion with the orbital circumference/time relation.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. A doubled period gives radius factor 2^(2/3), less than two.
q.feedback_incorrect: The orbit radius is measured from the planet centre, and the planet mass is unchanged.
q.explanation: Circular orbit periods scale as radius to the power three-halves for the same planet. Gravity supplies centripetal acceleration: v²=GM/r. Using v=2πr/T gives T²=4π²r³/(GM). Thus r_B/r_A=(T_B/T_A)^(2/3)=2^(2/3)=1.58740.

q.context: A uniform 4.0 m horizontal beam of mass 20 kg is hinged at its left end. A 30 kg load hangs 3.0 m from the hinge. A vertical cable supports the beam at its right end. Use g = 10 m/s².
q.prompt: Find the cable tension.
q.hint: Take torques about the hinge so its reaction has no lever arm.
q.feedback_incorrect: Do not place the uniform beam’s weight at its right end.
q.explanation: Beam weight acts at its midpoint, while the load acts at its stated position. The beam’s 200 N weight acts 2 m from the hinge; the 300 N load acts 3 m away. Torque balance gives 4T=20(10)(2)+30(10)(3)=1300, hence T=325 N. 4×325=200×2+300×3=1300 N·m.

q.context: A 2.00 kg block sits on a 4.00 kg block on a level floor. The top–bottom static friction coefficient is 0.400. The lower block is moving over the floor with kinetic friction coefficient 0.100. A horizontal force F pulls the upper block. Use g=10.0 m/s² and assume both blocks initially move together in the direction of the pull.
q.given: A 2.00 kg block sits on a 4.00 kg block on a level floor. The top–bottom static friction coefficient is 0.400. The lower block is moving over the floor with kinetic friction coefficient 0.100. A horizontal force F pulls the upper block. Use g=10.0 m/s² and assume both blocks initially move together in the direction of the pull.
q.prompt: Find the greatest F for which they can continue accelerating together without relative slipping.
q.find: Find the greatest F for which they can continue accelerating together without relative slipping.
q.hint: The lower block needs both acceleration force and force to overcome floor friction.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. At F=9 N, a=0.5 m/s² and inter-block friction is 8 N.
q.feedback_incorrect: The lower block cannot receive the applied F directly; it is pulled through inter-block friction.
q.explanation: The top interface has a finite static-friction capacity while the floor is sliding. The floor friction is 0.100×6.00×10.0=6.00 N on the lower block. For common acceleration a, the lower block needs inter-block friction f=4a+6, with limit 0.400×2×10=8.00 N. At the limit a=0.500 m/s²; the whole system requires F=6a+6=9.00 N.

q.context: A vehicle uses 600 W to maintain 10.0 m/s and 3600 W to maintain 20.0 m/s on level ground. Its resisting force is F₀+kv², with constant F₀ and k.
q.given: A vehicle uses 600 W to maintain 10.0 m/s and 3600 W to maintain 20.0 m/s on level ground. Its resisting force is F₀+kv², with constant F₀ and k.
q.prompt: Find the mechanical power needed at 15.0 m/s.
q.find: Find the mechanical power needed at 15.0 m/s.
q.hint: Convert each power to force before solving for the two resistance terms.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. F(15)=110 N, so P=1650 W.
q.feedback_incorrect: F₀ also consumes power; pure cubic scaling does not fit a nonzero constant resistance term.
q.explanation: At steady speed mechanical power is total resistance times speed. The two forces are 600/10=60.0 N and 3600/20=180 N. Subtracting F₀+100k=60 and F₀+400k=180 gives k=0.400 and F₀=20.0 N. At 15.0 m/s the resistance is 20.0+0.400×225=110 N, so power is 1650 W.

q.prompt: Find that maximum speed.
q.find: Find that maximum speed.
q.hint: At the high-speed limit friction points down the bank.
q.feedback_incorrect: Friction has both vertical and inward components; treating it as purely horizontal misses the coupled balance.
q.explanation: Resolve normal and limiting-friction components vertically and radially. At the upper limit friction acts down the bank: vertical balance is N cosθ−μN sinθ=mg. The inward force is N sinθ+μN cosθ=mv²/r. Divide to get v²/(rg)=(tanθ+μ)/(1−μtanθ). Substitute tanθ=0.500 and μ=0.200: v²=500×0.700/0.900, so v=19.7203 m/s.

q.find: Find the force magnitude at the first loss of static equilibrium.
q.prompt: Find the force magnitude at the first loss of static equilibrium.
q.hint: Calculate both possible thresholds with the downward force included.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The sliding threshold is 30/(cos 30°−0.25)=48.70 N, above the tipping threshold.
q.feedback_incorrect: A downward push increases the normal force and also produces a stabilising moment about the edge.
q.explanation: At impending rightward tipping, take moments about the lower right edge: F cos 30°(1.00)=0.400(60+F sin 30°). This gives F=24/(cos 30°−0.200)=36.0347 N. The required horizontal friction is 31.2069 N. The normal force is 78.0173 N, so the available friction is 39.0087 N. Tipping therefore occurs before sliding.

q.context: A uniform solid sphere and a frictionless sliding block start from rest at the same point on separate straight inclines of equal angle θ, length s and vertical drop h. The sphere rolls without slipping and has moment of inertia I=2mR²/5. Ignore air resistance and energy loss. The taught rolling constraint applies; both bodies reach the common lower height.
q.prompt: Find the sphere travel time divided by the block travel time. Enter a dimensionless ratio.
q.hint: Derive the two centre accelerations before comparing times over the same distance.
q.feedback_correct: The ratio exceeds1 and is independent of equal h, θ and both masses in this model.
q.feedback_incorrect: Energy equality alone does not state how energy is partitioned or determine equal travel times.
q.explanation: The slider has acceleration a_b=g sinθ. For a rolling sphere, mgh=½mv²+½I(v/R)²=7mv²/10, so v²=10gh/7. Because both straight inclines have h=s sinθ and constant acceleration, v²=2as gives a_s=5g sinθ/7. Static friction enforces rolling without slip; its contact point does no work in the ideal rigid model. From rest over equal path length s, t=√(2s/a). Hence t_s/t_b=√(a_b/a_s)=√(7/5). The ratio is 1.18321596: the sphere takes about18.3% longer. Translational and rotational kinetic energy share its gravitational loss.

q.find: Find the smallest static friction coefficient consistent with this observation.

q.context: A cart’s stopping distances at speeds 1, 2 and 3 m/s are in the ratio 1:4:9. A proposed model is constant opposing force; a second model says opposing force is proportional to speed.
q.given: A cart’s stopping distances at speeds 1, 2 and 3 m/s are in the ratio 1:4:9. A proposed model is constant opposing force; a second model says opposing force is proportional to speed.
q.prompt: Which independent check most directly distinguishes these models?
q.find: Which independent check most directly distinguishes these models?
q.hint: Compare the predicted time dependence of acceleration, not only one final distance.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Constant resistance gives a straight v–t segment; linear drag gives falling deceleration magnitude.
q.feedback_incorrect: A fitted distance scaling does not identify the microscopic friction mechanism uniquely.
q.explanation: Independent model consequences can distinguish constant resistance from speed-dependent drag. Constant opposing force gives kinetic energy removal Fd, hence d∝u². Linear drag instead gives acceleration proportional to current speed, so its time trace is not a straight line. A resolved velocity–time trace checks a different model consequence and can distinguish them within measurement uncertainty.

worked_solution.check: The proposed axes match P=K(1/V) directly and control the quantities assumed constant.

worked_solution.model: At equal P and T, PV=Nk_BT makes particle number N proportional to volume. N counts molecules here and k_B is the Boltzmann constant.

Equal pressures and temperatures cancel.
worked_solution.check: The larger sample has 2.5 times the volume at the same particle density, so it should contain 2.5 times as many molecules.
worked_solution.common_error: Assuming equal pressure and temperature imply equal particle number regardless of volume.

q.prompt: Find the final gauge pressure. Atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa.
q.hint: Convert the initial gauge pressure to absolute pressure before using Boyle’s law.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The final absolute pressure is 180 kPa, so the gauge pressure is 80 kPa.
q.feedback_incorrect: Gas laws use absolute pressure. Add atmospheric pressure first and subtract it at the end.
q.explanation: P₁(abs)=35+100=135 kPa. P₂(abs)=135×600/450=180 kPa, hence P₂(gauge)=80 kPa.
q.context: A sealed syringe reads 35 kPa gauge at 600 cm³. It is compressed slowly and isothermally to 450 cm³.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Gauge pressure versus absolute pressure
worked_solution.model: Boyle’s law requires absolute pressure. Convert before the calculation and convert back afterwards.
steps: Initial absolute pressure: P₁=35+100=135 kPa.
Slow isothermal compression: P₂(abs)=135×600/450=180 kPa.
Final gauge pressure: 180−100=80 kPa.
worked_solution.check: A smaller volume gives a larger absolute pressure; the final gauge value is positive and below the 180 kPa absolute value.
worked_solution.common_error: Putting 35 kPa directly into Boyle’s law.

q.prompt: Which method gives the fairest test of Boyle’s law?
options: Compress rapidly and record the peak pressure at each volume.
Use gauge pressure and ignore the volume of the tubing.
Change volume in steps, wait for thermal equilibrium, and plot absolute pressure against reciprocal total volume.
Open the syringe between readings to reset the pressure.
q.hint: Control temperature and use the physical quantities that appear in the model.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. This controls temperature and tests the predicted linear relationship using absolute quantities.
q.feedback_incorrect: A fair Boyle’s-law test needs constant temperature, fixed gas amount, absolute pressure and total gas volume.
q.explanation: Waiting removes transient heating. For fixed n and T, P is proportional to 1/V, where V includes all trapped gas.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Designing a valid Boyle’s-law experiment
worked_solution.model: The model assumes fixed n and T and uses absolute pressure and actual trapped volume.
steps: Change volume in steps without opening the gas system.
Wait after each change so compression heating or expansion cooling disappears.
Measure absolute pressure and include tubing dead volume.
Plot P against 1/V_total and inspect linearity and intercept.
worked_solution.check: This procedure controls temperature and tests the exact linearised model.
worked_solution.common_error: Recording rapid peak pressures, which mixes thermal transients with the volume effect.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Particle explanation of gas pressure
worked_solution.model: Temperature measures average random kinetic energy. Pressure results from momentum transfer during wall collisions.
steps: Heating increases the particles’ average kinetic energy and speed.
Faster particles reach the walls more frequently.
Each collision produces a larger momentum change on average.

q.context: A syringe is compressed rapidly and clamped. Its pressure jumps from 100 kPa to 230 kPa, then falls to 190 kPa over one minute while the measured volume stays fixed. The gas is sealed with no reaction. The first and final settled states are at the same measured room temperature; the later 190 kPa reading is taken after thermal equilibrium. All pressures are absolute.
q.prompt: Explain the complete pressure history using the particle model and state which reading is suitable for a Boyle-law test.
q.hint: Link work, temperature, particle collisions and the measurement condition in one causal chain.
q.feedback_correct: Good. The explanation links the physical model to the evidence.
q.feedback_partial: The main idea is present, but one or more links in the reasoning chain are missing.
q.feedback_incorrect: Link work, temperature, particle collisions and the measurement condition in one causal chain.
q.explanation: Rapid work raises temperature and collision momentum, causing the pressure overshoot. At fixed volume the gas then transfers energy to the surroundings, particles slow and pressure falls. The settled 190 kPa reading is appropriate for an approximately isothermal Boyle-law comparison.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Thermal transient in a Boyle’s-law measurement
worked_solution.model: Rapid compression is not isothermal; the later settled reading is closer to the controlled-temperature state.
steps: Work done during rapid compression raises internal energy and temperature.
Faster particles produce the 230 kPa pressure overshoot.
While clamped, the gas loses thermal energy at fixed volume and pressure falls.
After thermal equilibrium, 190 kPa is the suitable Boyle-law reading.
worked_solution.check: A Boyle comparison requires equal temperatures; the later reading is the one taken after that condition is approximately restored.
worked_solution.common_error: Treating the immediate peak as the isothermal pressure.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Finding hidden dead volume
worked_solution.model: The actual trapped volume is the syringe reading plus the same unknown dead volume d in both states.
steps: Apply Boyle’s law: 100(80+d)=160(40+d).

worked_solution.check: Substitution gives equal products: 100×106.67≈160×66.67≈10667 kPa·cm³.
worked_solution.common_error: Adding d to one state only or assigning it a negative sign.

q.context: A pressure sensor has a constant zero offset b, so true pressure is P_read+b. The same gas at constant temperature reads 90 kPa at 100 cm³ and 190 kPa at 50 cm³. Dead volume is negligible.

q.explanation: Boyle's law gives (90+b)100=(190+b)50, so b=10 kPa.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Finding a constant pressure offset
worked_solution.model: True absolute pressure equals the displayed value plus the same offset b at every reading.
steps: Set the Boyle products equal: (90+b)100=(190+b)50.

worked_solution.check: Corrected pressures are 100 and 200 kPa while volumes are 100 and 50 cm³, giving equal PV.
worked_solution.common_error: Applying the offset to only one pressure reading.

q.context: Repeated compression data drift downward. The apparatus might be warming temporarily, leaking slowly or suffering a sensor offset.
q.prompt: Design a measurement sequence that separates the three causes and state the diagnostic pattern for each.
q.hint: Use time dependence, repeatability and an independent calibration standard.
q.feedback_correct: Good. The explanation links the physical model to the evidence.
q.feedback_partial: The main idea is present, but one or more links in the reasoning chain are missing.
q.feedback_incorrect: Use time dependence, repeatability and an independent calibration standard.
q.explanation: Wait at each volume and monitor temperature to expose thermal transients; return repeatedly to the same reference volume to reveal irreversible gas loss; check the sensor at a known pressure to identify a fixed offset. Heating decays with time, leakage produces progressive non-recovery and an offset remains reproducible.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Separating thermal drift, leakage and sensor offset
worked_solution.model: Use time behaviour, return-to-reference cycles and independent calibration because the three faults leave different signatures.
steps: At each volume, record pressure and temperature versus time; a thermal transient decays as equilibrium returns.
Cycle repeatedly back to the same reference volume; leakage causes progressive failure to recover the original settled pressure.
Check the sensor against known atmospheric pressure or another calibrated standard; a zero offset remains reproducible.
Repeat the sequence to distinguish random scatter from systematic patterns.
worked_solution.final_answer: Heating decays with time; leakage accumulates between cycles; offset is constant against a standard.
worked_solution.check: The design creates an independent observation for each proposed cause.
worked_solution.common_error: Changing several conditions at once and then assigning all drift to leakage.

q.prompt: Which explanation and follow-up measurement are most consistent with these facts?
q.find: Which explanation and follow-up measurement are most consistent with these facts?

q.feedback_correct: Correct. The required internal pressure is about 1.33 times the pressure used in the freely flexible calculation.
q.feedback_incorrect: Do not assume a mechanical approximation has been verified merely because the gas equation is familiar.
q.explanation: At equal amount and temperature, reducing volume from 8.0 to 6.0 L requires a pressure factor 8/6. A taut membrane can provide a pressure difference; it need not follow the negligible-tension approximation. Measuring the internal–external pressure difference tests this additional mechanical constraint.

q.feedback_incorrect: Two particles replace each reacting molecule, but the molecules that did not react still count as one each. Doubling occurs only for 100% dissociation.
q.explanation: Let N₀ be the original number of A₂ molecules. The fraction x splits, so xN₀ molecules react and (1−x)N₀ stay intact. Each reacting molecule produces two atoms: 2xN₀ free A atoms. Only 30% of the original molecules split. Check the atom count: 2(1−x)N₀+2xN₀=2N₀. Particle count changes while atoms and mass are conserved.

q.find: Calculate the upward displacement, in cm.
q.hint: Write a piston force balance and convert litres to cubic metres before forming one equation.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The final pressure exceeds 100 kPa; assuming constant pressure would predict too much expansion.
q.feedback_incorrect: The spring force is kx, not a constant load; do not use constant-pressure expansion.
q.explanation: For an upward displacement x in metres, force balance gives P=100000+500x/0.010 Pa. The gas volume is V=0.00200+0.010x m³; conserving PV/T gives PV=100000×0.00200×450/300=300 J. Expanding yields 500x²+1100x−100=0, with the physical positive root x=0.0874342 m. The displacement is 8.74342 cm; the other root would give an invalid volume and direction.

q.given: A massless vertical piston of area 0.010 m² traps 2.00 L of ideal gas at 300 K. The exterior pressure is 100 kPa. A spring above the piston is initially relaxed and is compressed when the piston rises; its stiffness is 500 N/m. Heat the sealed gas slowly to 450 K. Ignore friction and assume no stop is reached.
q.prompt: Calculate the upward displacement, in cm.
q.find: Calculate the upward displacement, in cm.
q.hint: Write a piston force balance and convert litres to cubic metres before forming one equation.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The final pressure exceeds 100 kPa; assuming constant pressure would predict too much expansion.
q.feedback_incorrect: The spring force is kx, not a constant load; do not use constant-pressure expansion.
q.explanation: For an upward displacement x in metres, force balance gives P=100000+500x/0.010 Pa. The gas volume is V=0.00200+0.010x m³; conserving PV/T gives PV=100000×0.00200×450/300=300 J. Expanding yields 500x²+1100x−100=0, with the physical positive root x=0.0874342 m. The displacement is 8.74342 cm; the other root would give an invalid volume and direction.

q.context: A uniform tube is sealed at one end and contains a fixed air sample separated from the atmosphere by a 0.200 m mercury plug. At the same temperature, the trapped-air length is 0.400 m when the sealed end is above the plug, and 0.240 m when the sealed end is below it. Mercury density is 13000 kg/m³; g=10.0 m/s². Ignore capillary effects and air weight.
q.given: A uniform tube is sealed at one end and contains a fixed air sample separated from the atmosphere by a 0.200 m mercury plug. At the same temperature, the trapped-air length is 0.400 m when the sealed end is above the plug, and 0.240 m when the sealed end is below it. Mercury density is 13000 kg/m³; g=10.0 m/s². Ignore capillary effects and air weight.
q.prompt: Determine atmospheric pressure, in kPa.
q.find: Determine atmospheric pressure, in kPa.
q.hint: Locate the gas–mercury interface relative to the exposed end of the mercury plug in each orientation.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The gas pressures are 78 and 130 kPa, and 78×0.400=130×0.240.
q.feedback_incorrect: Applying the same sign of mercury head in both orientations destroys the information needed to infer atmosphere.
q.explanation: The mercury head is ρgh=13000×10×0.200=26000 Pa=26.0 kPa. With gas above the plug its pressure is P_atm−26; with gas below the plug it is P_atm+26. Boyle’s law gives (P_atm−26)×0.400=(P_atm+26)×0.240. Solving 0.160P_atm=16.64 gives P_atm=104 kPa.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Inferring atmospheric pressure from two orientations
worked_solution.model: Reversing the tube reverses the sign of the hydrostatic pressure difference. The two air volumes share the same area.
steps: The mercury head is ρgh=13000×10×0.200=26000 Pa=26.0 kPa.
With gas above the plug its pressure is P_atm−26; with gas below the plug it is P_atm+26.
Boyle’s law gives (P_atm−26)×0.400=(P_atm+26)×0.240.
Solving 0.160P_atm=16.64 gives P_atm=104 kPa.
worked_solution.check: The gas pressures are 78 and 130 kPa, and 78×0.400=130×0.240.
worked_solution.common_error: Applying the same sign of mercury head in both orientations destroys the information needed to infer atmosphere.

application_brief.background: The mercury plug separates trapped air from open atmosphere. Pressure increases from the higher face of a stationary liquid plug to its lower face. The plug is vertical in both trials; its 0.200 m length is the vertical separation of its two faces. Follow which face touches trapped air before choosing a pressure sign.

variables.meaning: Vertical height of the mercury plug.
Length occupied by trapped air in a tube of fixed cross-sectional area.

conditions: Air cannot pass the mercury plug; compare the same trapped sample at the same temperature.
The two tube orientations are shown schematically; do not infer a length from the drawing.

figures.caption: Original schematic. The mercury head is the vertical distance between the plug faces; the general hydrostatic law was taught in the Concept Brief.

q.context: A rigid vessel initially contains only A₂ at 300 K. A fraction x dissociates to 2A; afterwards a fraction f of the gas particles escapes without selecting either species. At 360 K the final pressure is 1.20 times the initial pressure. No other reactions occur. Use ideal-gas behaviour. As defined in Core 2, A is one atom and A₂ is a molecule containing two A atoms. The fraction x refers to original molecules, while f refers to all particles present immediately after dissociation; 0≤x,f≤1.
q.given: A rigid vessel initially contains only A₂ at 300 K. A fraction x dissociates to 2A; afterwards a fraction f of the gas particles escapes without selecting either species. At 360 K the final pressure is 1.20 times the initial pressure. No other reactions occur. Use ideal-gas behaviour. As defined in Core 2, A is one atom and A₂ is a molecule containing two A atoms. The fraction x refers to original molecules, while f refers to all particles present immediately after dissociation; 0≤x,f≤1.
q.prompt: Which conclusion and additional observation are justified?
q.find: Which conclusion and additional observation are justified?
q.hint: Write the separate particle-number factors for reaction and escape before combining them.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. A 25% particle increase followed by losing 20% of that larger population returns the count to its starting value. The gas mass is nevertheless 20% lower.
q.feedback_incorrect: Mass conservation during a reaction does not imply particle-number conservation; pressure alone cannot separate both processes.
q.explanation: Use the Core particle count: from N₀ original molecules, dissociation leaves (1+x)N₀ particles. The same atoms are redistributed between molecules and free atoms. Escaping fraction f removes f of this new particle population. The retained number is N_final=(1−f)(1+x)N₀. The fixed-volume ideal-gas law gives P_final/P_initial=(N_final/N₀)(T_final/T_initial)=(1−f)(1+x)×360/300. Divide the observed 1.20 pressure ratio by 360/300=1.20: (1+x)(1−f)=1. This single equation cannot determine two unknown fractions. For example, x=f=0 and x=0.25, f=0.20 both fit: 1.25×0.80=1. Weigh the gas before and after. Dissociation changes bonding and particle number without losing atoms; escape removes mass. Under the stated nonselective escape model, retained mass/original mass=1−f, providing a second independent constraint.

worked_solution.tested_idea: What pressure alone cannot identify
worked_solution.model: Pressure gives a particle-number constraint, not separate dissociation and leakage fractions. Escaping material changes mass; dissociation alone does not.

options: The pressure ratio proves that neither dissociation nor leakage occurred; another measurement cannot change that.
The pressure ratio proves x=0.20 and f=0; measure volume to confirm it.

Only x−f=0 is fixed for all fractions; retained mass would be unchanged even if gas escaped.

q.given: A rigid insulated enclosure connects chamber A (2.0 L, 150 kPa, 300 K) to chamber B (1.0 L, 250 kPa, 500 K). Both hold the same ideal monatomic gas. No gas escapes and the walls have negligible heat capacity. For this gas the internal energy is U=(3/2)nRT. After connection the gas reaches one common temperature and pressure.
q.prompt: Calculate the final temperature, in K.
q.find: Calculate the final temperature, in K.
q.hint: Use the supplied energy model as well as the gas equation; the final temperature has not been supplied.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The two gas amounts are in the ratio 2:1, so their amount-weighted temperature lies nearer 300 K.
q.feedback_incorrect: Averaging 300 K and 500 K equally ignores the unequal amounts in the chambers.
q.explanation: The outer enclosure is insulated and rigid. There is no heat input or external volume work, so gas energy is conserved; no gas escapes, so total amount is also conserved. For each initial region nR=PV/T. Hence n_A R=150×2/300=1.00 and n_B R=250×1/500=0.500 kPa L/K; total nR=1.50 kPa L/K. Using PV=nRT in the supplied model gives U=(3/2)PV. Initially U_total=(3/2)(150×2+250×1)=825 J, since 1 kPa L=1 J. At the final common temperature U_total=(3/2)(n_total R)T_final. Therefore T_final=825/[(3/2)×1.50]=366.667 K. The final pressure, if checked, is (1.50×366.667)/(2.0+1.0)=183.333 kPa.

For an ideal gas with constant molar heat capacity at fixed volume C_V, a temperature change gives ΔU=nC_VΔT. Here n is amount in mol, C_V is energy per mole per kelvin in J/(mol K), and ΔT is in K. Total heat capacity is nC_V in J/K; mass-specific c is in J/(kg K). Different ideal gases may have different C_V. For a monatomic ideal gas C_V=3R/2; choose one common energy reference. In a rigid insulated mixing system there is no external work or heat, so total internal energy is conserved.

grade.feedback: Averaging 300 K and 500 K equally ignores the unequal amounts in the chambers.
grade.explanation: The outer enclosure is insulated and rigid. There is no heat input or external volume work, so gas energy is conserved; no gas escapes, so total amount is also conserved. For each initial region nR=PV/T. Hence n_A R=150×2/300=1.00 and n_B R=250×1/500=0.500 kPa L/K; total nR=1.50 kPa L/K. Using PV=nRT in the supplied model gives U=(3/2)PV. Initially U_total=(3/2)(150×2+250×1)=825 J, since 1 kPa L=1 J. At the final common temperature U_total=(3/2)(n_total R)T_final. Therefore T_final=825/[(3/2)×1.50]=366.667 K. The final pressure, if checked, is (1.50×366.667)/(2.0+1.0)=183.333 kPa.

q.given: An isothermal gas apparatus has indicated gas volumes V and unknown fixed extra volume d. With no leakage, P(V+d) is constant. Measurements are (V=100 cm³,P=180 kPa) and (V=200 cm³,P=100 kPa). A third measurement at V=300 cm³ gives 67.5 kPa at the same temperature. Pressures are absolute; connecting volumes remain fixed.
q.context: An isothermal gas apparatus has indicated gas volumes V and unknown fixed extra volume d. With no leakage, P(V+d) is constant. Measurements are (V=100 cm³,P=180 kPa) and (V=200 cm³,P=100 kPa). A third measurement at V=300 cm³ gives 67.5 kPa at the same temperature. Pressures are absolute; connecting volumes remain fixed.
q.find: Using the first two readings as calibration, find the percentage of gas particles lost before the third reading.
q.prompt: Using the first two readings as calibration, find the percentage of gas particles lost before the third reading.
q.hint: Fit the apparatus from the first two states, then treat the last state as independent evidence.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. A no-leak prediction is 69.2308 kPa, above the measured pressure.
q.feedback_incorrect: Fitting all three readings with a different dead volume can conceal a loss after calibration.
q.explanation: Calibration gives 180(100+d)=100(200+d), so d=25 cm³ and the initial invariant is 22500 kPa cm³. The third invariant using the same d is 67.5(300+25)=21937.5 kPa cm³. At fixed temperature invariant is proportional to particle number, so loss=100(1−21937.5/22500)=2.50%.

q.context: A sealed ideal-gas estimate gives P=100 kPa, V=1.00 L and T=300 K. Boltzmann constant is k_B=1.38×10⁻²³ J/K. Approximate each molecule as a sphere of diameter 4.00×10⁻¹⁰ m, with sphere volume πd³/6. During isothermal compression the particle number stays fixed. Define a finite-size warning when these sphere volumes occupy 1.00% of the container.
q.given: A sealed ideal-gas estimate gives P=100 kPa, V=1.00 L and T=300 K. Boltzmann constant is k_B=1.38×10⁻²³ J/K. Approximate each molecule as a sphere of diameter 4.00×10⁻¹⁰ m, with sphere volume πd³/6. During isothermal compression the particle number stays fixed. Define a finite-size warning when these sphere volumes occupy 1.00% of the container.
q.prompt: At what container volume, in cm³, is this warning reached? This criterion tests finite size only, not all causes of non-ideal behaviour.
q.find: At what container volume, in cm³, is this warning reached? This criterion tests finite size only, not all causes of non-ideal behaviour.
q.hint: The warning refers to the sum of molecular volumes, not to the spacing between two neighbouring molecules.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The warning volume is smaller than 1000 cm³; small finite-size fraction alone does not rule out intermolecular attractions.
q.feedback_incorrect: Cube the molecular diameter and keep cubic-metre to cubic-centimetre conversion separate from the percent conversion.
q.explanation: PV=Nk_BT gives N=100000×0.00100/(1.38×10⁻²³×300)=2.41546×10²². The summed sphere volume is Nπd³/6≈8.09428×10⁻⁷ m³. At a 0.0100 fraction the container volume is about 8.09428×10⁻⁵ m³=80.9428 cm³.

worked_solution.tested_idea: A finite-size warning threshold
worked_solution.model: Infer the absolute particle number, add molecular sphere volumes, then solve a volume-fraction constraint.
steps: The summed sphere volume is Nπd³/6≈8.09428×10⁻⁷ m³.
At a 0.0100 fraction the container volume is about 8.09428×10⁻⁵ m³=80.9428 cm³.

q.context: A uniform vertical tube is sealed at the top and open at the bottom. Initially its open bottom just touches the water surface and air at 100 kPa absolute fills its 0.500 m length, with the sealed top above the water. Lower the tube until its top is 2.00 m below the water surface. Temperature stays constant; no air escapes. Use water density 1000 kg/m³ and g=9.8 m/s². Ignore capillary effects. Water can enter through the bottom.
q.prompt: How far does water rise inside the tube?
q.hint: Choose the unknown trapped-air length, locate the interface depth, then apply the pressure and volume laws.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Boyle's law gives [100+9.8(2+L)]L=100×0.50. The physical root is L=0.4046 m, so water rises 0.500−0.4046=0.0954 m.
q.feedback_incorrect: The gas-water interface depth contains the unknown L, so form and solve an equation before finding the rise.
q.explanation: Let L be the final trapped-air length in metres. The total tube length stays 0.500 m, so the water rise to report is 0.500−L. The gas–water interface lies L below the sealed top, which is itself 2.00 m below the lake surface. Its depth is therefore h=2.00+L. Hydrostatic equilibrium gives P_final=100+9.8(2.00+L) kPa. Isothermal fixed gas gives P_initial A(0.500)=P_final AL, with tube area A cancelling. Expand: [100+9.8(2.00+L)]L=50, or 9.8L²+119.6L−50=0. Use L=[−119.6+√(119.6²+4×9.8×50)]/(2×9.8)=0.4046 m. The negative root is not an air length. The rise is 0.5000−0.4046=0.0954 m=9.54 cm.

steps: Use a rigid sealed bulb, calibrated absolute-pressure sensor and independent calibrated temperature standard.

q.given: A sealed frictionless piston maintains total pressure 100 kPa. Initially at 300 K it contains 0.0400 mol of a noncondensing ideal gas (one that stays gaseous throughout) and 0.0200 mol total of substance X, initially supplied as liquid. X saturated vapour pressure is 20.0 kPa at 300 K and 40.0 kPa at 400 K. If liquid remains in equilibrium, X vapour partial pressure equals its saturation value. Otherwise all X is vapour with partial pressure n_XRT/V. Each gas partial pressure is n_iRT/V and partial pressures add. Heat slowly to 400 K. Liquid volume is negligible; use R=8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. A partial pressure is the pressure contribution of one gas species; equilibrium means the final macroscopic state is no longer changing.

Otherwise all X is vapour with partial pressure n_XRT/V. Each gas partial pressure is n_iRT/V and partial pressures add. Heat slowly to 400 K. Liquid volume is negligible; use R=8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. A partial pressure is the pressure contribution of one gas species; equilibrium means the final macroscopic state is no longer changing.
q.find: Find final volume divided by initial equilibrium volume.
q.prompt: Find final volume divided by initial equilibrium volume.
q.hint: Check available liquid against the vapour amount needed for each candidate equilibrium.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The final X partial pressure is 100×0.0200/0.0600=33.333 kPa, below saturation 40 kPa, consistent with full evaporation.
q.feedback_incorrect: Applying the saturated pressure at both temperatures assumes an unlimited liquid supply.
q.explanation: At 300 K, saturation would require n_X/n_air=20/80=0.250, hence 0.0100 mol vapour. Enough X exists, and V_initial=0.0400R(300)/80. At 400 K, retaining liquid would require n_X=0.0400(40/60)=0.026667 mol, more than the 0.0200 mol available; all X evaporates. Final volume is(0.0400+0.0200)R(400)/100. Dividing by the initial volume gives 1.60.

q.context: A rigid 4.00 L gas supply starts at 250 kPa absolute and 300 K. A valve releases gas under water at a depth of 5.00 m, then closes when internal pressure equals local water pressure. Surface atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa; use water density 1000 kg/m³ and g=10.0 m/s². The final settled gas is also at 300 K and its mass has decreased by 4.80 g. Assume ideal-gas behaviour and unchanged composition; R=8.314 J/(mol K).
q.given: A rigid 4.00 L gas supply starts at 250 kPa absolute and 300 K. A valve releases gas under water at a depth of 5.00 m, then closes when internal pressure equals local water pressure. Surface atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa; use water density 1000 kg/m³ and g=10.0 m/s². The final settled gas is also at 300 K and its mass has decreased by 4.80 g. Assume ideal-gas behaviour and unchanged composition; R=8.314 J/(mol K).
q.prompt: Infer the molar mass of the released gas, in g/mol.
q.find: Infer the molar mass of the released gas, in g/mol.
q.hint: Find how much gas left from the two states of the fixed vessel, then compare that amount with the measured mass loss.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Using the initial amount instead of the released amount would not match the measured mass difference.
q.feedback_incorrect: A mass difference belongs with a particle-amount difference, not with the initial total amount.
q.explanation: The valve closes at the water pressure. P_after=P_atm+ρgh=100+1000×10.0×5.00/1000=150 kPa absolute. Before and after, volume and settled temperature are the same. Subtract n_before=P_before V/(RT) and n_after=P_after V/(RT), giving Δn=(P_before−P_after)V/(RT). Convert units for R in joules: ΔP=100000 Pa and V=0.00400 m³. Then Δn=100000×0.00400/(8.314×300)=0.160372 mol. Molar mass is mass per mole of the same released gas: M=Δm/Δn=4.80 g/0.160372 mol=29.9304 g/mol.

q.context: Rigid chamber A (1.00 L) initially contains only helium at 200 kPa; chamber B (2.00 L) initially contains only neon at 100 kPa. Both are kept at 300 K. q.given: Rigid chamber A (1.00 L) initially contains only helium at 200 kPa; chamber B (2.00 L) initially contains only neon at 100 kPa. Both are kept at 300 K. Their connecting membrane passes helium but not neon. At final equilibrium helium has the same partial pressure on both sides. For ideal mixtures, total pressure is the sum of partial pressures. No gas escapes.
q.prompt: Calculate the final total pressure in chamber B, in kPa.
q.find: Calculate the final total pressure in chamber B, in kPa.
q.hint: Identify what can cross the boundary before choosing the equilibrium condition.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Equal helium partial pressures do not imply equal total pressures across a selective membrane.
q.feedback_incorrect: Treating the membrane as an unrestricted valve incorrectly moves neon and equalises total pressure.
q.explanation: Use p_i V=n_i RT for each species separately. Helium can enter both rigid chambers, so its final available volume is 1.00+2.00=3.00 L at the same 300 K. Conserved helium amount gives p_He(final)×3.00=200×1.00, so p_He(final)=66.6667 kPa in each chamber. Neon cannot cross the membrane. Its amount, original 2.00 L volume and temperature stay fixed, so its partial pressure in B stays 100 kPa. The wall in B receives both independent contributions: P_B=p_He+p_Ne=66.6667+100=166.667 kPa.

application_brief.background: A selective membrane is a barrier with different permeability to different species. Here helium atoms can cross and neon atoms cannot. Partial pressure has the meaning introduced in Core 2: the contribution of one species to the total wall pressure. A membrane held by the chamber can support different total pressures on its two sides.

variables.meaning: Helium and neon partial pressures in a chosen chamber.

conditions: The membrane is fixed and the chamber volumes do not change.
The supplied equilibrium condition equalises helium partial pressure only. It does not equalise the two total pressures.

difficulty_calibration.rationale: 膜选择性只约束氦，需分物种守恒并叠加分压。
difficulty_calibration.demand_scheme: r12 common content bands: D1 recall/routine; D2 model application; D3 linked reasoning; D4 coupled/inverse/evidence integration

grade.feedback: Treating the membrane as an unrestricted valve incorrectly moves neon and equalises total pressure.
grade.explanation: Use p_i V=n_i RT for each species separately. Helium can enter both rigid chambers, so its final available volume is 1.00+2.00=3.00 L at the same 300 K. Conserved helium amount gives p_He(final)×3.00=200×1.00, so p_He(final)=66.6667 kPa in each chamber. Neon cannot cross the membrane. Its amount, original 2.00 L volume and temperature stay fixed, so its partial pressure in B stays 100 kPa. The wall in B receives both independent contributions: P_B=p_He+p_Ne=66.6667+100=166.667 kPa.

q.context: A sealed gas sensor is at 100 kPa absolute, 1.000 L and 300 K. At 400 K its measured pressure is 120 kPa. The container obeys V=V₀[1+α(T−300 K)], where V₀=1.000 L and α is an unknown volume-expansion coefficient. Assume ideal gas, uniform temperature and no leakage. This is the same first-order housing model introduced with the gas thermometer; α measures fractional volume increase per kelvin relative to 300 K.

q.given: A rigid tank initially contains 10.0 g of ideal gas at 100 kPa absolute and 300 K. A valve opens only if pressure would exceed 150 kPa, then releases gas to maintain 150 kPa. Heat slowly to 600 K and cool back to 300 K. The valve admits no gas; neglect volume changes and temperature gradients.
q.context: A rigid tank initially contains 10.0 g of ideal gas at 100 kPa absolute and 300 K. A valve opens only if pressure would exceed 150 kPa, then releases gas to maintain 150 kPa. Heat slowly to 600 K and cool back to 300 K. The valve admits no gas; neglect volume changes and temperature gradients.
q.find: Find the final absolute pressure.
q.prompt: Find the final absolute pressure.
q.hint: Locate the switching temperature and track mass through each stage.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The final tank is below its original pressure because mass escaped during only the high-temperature part.
q.feedback_incorrect: The valve is a one-way upper-pressure constraint, not a permanent 150 kPa boundary.
q.explanation: Before venting, pressure is proportional to temperature; the valve first opens at 450 K. At 600 K the retained mass is 10×(150/100)×(300/600)=7.50 g. On cooling the outward valve closes, leaving fixed mass; final pressure is 150×300/600=75.0 kPa.

q.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy gained by the water.
q.hint: Identify the temperature change of the water, then use its mass and specific heat.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The sample heat capacity is 2100 J/K; 30 K therefore requires 63000 J. The absorbed energy is positive.

q.context: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed in an insulated container. The cup heat capacity and environmental heat exchange are negligible; take the same constant c for both samples.
q.given: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed in an insulated container. The cup heat capacity and environmental heat exchange are negligible; take the same constant c for both samples.
q.find: Find the final equilibrium temperature.

worked_solution.model: The two water portions form an insulated system with negligible cup storage. Equal mass and equal c give equal whole-sample heat capacities.

q.prompt: Calculate the energy required to melt the ice without changing its temperature.
q.hint: Name the phase change and use only the mass undergoing that change.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. kg cancels against kg in kJ/kg, leaving the requested kJ.
q.feedback_incorrect: A zero temperature change does not imply zero energy transfer during melting.
q.explanation: The required energy is latent fusion energy; there is no initial ice-warming or final water-warming stage. Use Q=mL_f=(0.20 kg)(334 kJ/kg)=66.8 kJ. The energy is absorbed by the ice-water system while the liquid fraction rises from zero to one.

q.prompt: Which surface is the best thermal-radiation emitter?
options: Polished silver
Shiny white
Dull black
All surfaces emit equally at the same temperature
q.hint: Identify which surface property multiplies the emitted radiation at fixed area and temperature.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The comparison changes ε while keeping A and T fixed; latent heat is irrelevant here.
q.feedback_incorrect: Visible colour alone is not a universal infrared emissivity measurement; use the stated surface model.
q.explanation: At fixed emitting area and absolute temperature, P_emit=εσAT⁴ changes in proportion to emissivity ε. The ordinary dull black coating is the high-emissivity finish in these choices; polished reflective finishes have lower thermal emission in this model. Choose Option 3. Equal temperature alone does not make the emitted powers equal; phase-change formulae do not apply to this comparison.
q.given: Four surface finishes at the same temperature are listed in the answer choices. Compare equal emitting areas and use the usual school-laboratory thermal-radiation model for these surface finishes.
q.find: Which surface is the best thermal-radiation emitter?

q.given: A surface at 400 K emits 60.0 W of thermal radiation and has a net radiative loss of 45.0 W in a large isothermal enclosure. The surface and enclosure exchange radiation according to P_net=εσA(T⁴−T_s⁴), with P_emitted=εσAT⁴. The same ε and effective area apply to absorption and emission.
q.prompt: Infer the enclosure temperature T_s, in K.
q.find: Infer the enclosure temperature T_s, in K.
q.hint: Separate incoming absorbed power from the measured net outgoing power before forming a ratio.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The surroundings are cooler than the 400 K surface, consistent with positive net loss.
q.feedback_incorrect: Net loss is not the full emitted power; some radiation returns from the enclosure.
q.explanation: Net loss=emitted−absorbed, so P_absorbed=60.0−45.0=15.0 W. The common εσA cancels when dividing P_absorbed=εσAT_s⁴ by P_emitted=εσA(400 K)⁴. (T_s/400)⁴=15.0/60.0=0.250, giving T_s=400×0.250^(1/4)=282.843 K. Use the positive fourth root because T_s is an absolute temperature.

q.context: A device in a 20 °C room has accurate steady measurements: input power 10, 20 and 40 W gives temperature rises above the room of 10, 20 and 30 K respectively. Each rise has uncertainty ±0.5 K; input power uncertainty is negligible. A proposed model is P_loss=k(T−T_room) with one constant k.
q.given: A device in a 20 °C room has accurate steady measurements: input power 10, 20 and 40 W gives temperature rises above the room of 10, 20 and 30 K respectively. Each rise has uncertainty ±0.5 K; input power uncertainty is negligible. A proposed model is P_loss=k(T−T_room) with one constant k.
q.prompt: Which interpretation is supported by all three measurements?
q.find: Which interpretation is supported by all three measurements?
q.hint: A shared parameter must agree across all trials, not just the two lowest powers.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The full uncertainty intervals cannot rescue one constant k.
q.feedback_incorrect: A failed linear fit does not by itself prove radiation is the unique missing mechanism.
q.explanation: The first two central readings give k=10/10=20/20=1.00 W/K. This model predicts ΔT=40/1.00=40 K at 40 W, outside the observed 30±0.5 K range. Even the first reading’s full k range, 10/10.5 to 10/9.5=0.952–1.053 W/K, does not overlap the third reading’s 40/30.5 to 40/29.5=1.311–1.356 W/K. Choose Option 3. A stronger temperature-dependent loss is possible, but the data do not uniquely identify its mechanism.

worked_solution.model: Each steady reading equates input with loss. A single constant coefficient must fit all temperature differences within their uncertainties.

q.given: The same 0.200 kg metal block starts at 100 °C in each of two trials. In trial A it is placed in 0.300 kg of water initially at 20 °C in a cup, also at 20 °C; final temperature is 25 °C. In trial B use 0.100 kg water in the same cup at 20 °C; final temperature is 30 °C. The cup heat capacity C and metal specific heat c are unknown constants. Use c_water=4200 J/(kg K); neglect all environmental heat exchange.
q.prompt: Infer the cup heat capacity C, in J/K.
q.find: Infer the cup heat capacity C, in J/K.
q.hint: Use the same two unknown properties in both energy accounts; eliminate one algebraically.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Both inferred properties are positive and recover both independent trial results.
q.feedback_incorrect: Treating the two trials as if the cup had different unknown capacities removes the shared constraint.
q.explanation: Trial A: metal release 0.200c(100−25) equals water-plus-cup gain (0.300×4200+C)(25−20), so 15c=6300+5C. Trial B: 0.200c(100−30)=(0.100×4200+C)(30−20), giving 14c=4200+10C. Divide the first equation by 5: C=3c−1260. Substitute into the second: 14c=4200+30c−12600, hence 16c=8400 and c=525 J/(kg K). C=3×525−1260=315 J/K. Trial A transfers 7875 J and Trial B transfers 7350 J; each matches its water-plus-cup gain.

q.given: An insulated container with negligible heat capacity initially holds 0.100 kg water at 20 °C and 0.050 kg ice at 0 °C. Add a 1.00 kg metal block at −50 °C, with c_metal=500 J/(kg K). Use c_water=4200 J/(kg K), c_ice=2100 J/(kg K), and L_f=334000 J/kg. Ignore environmental exchange.

q.hint: Compare energy supply and demand at the phase boundary; the sign decides melting versus freezing.

q.feedback_incorrect: Report total final ice, including the original ice; do not assume every mixing problem melts ice.
q.explanation: Cooling the initial water to 0 °C releases 0.100×4200×20=8400 J. The metal needs 1.00×500×50=25000 J to warm to 0 °C, leaving a deficit of 16600 J. Final ice includes the original 0.050 kg plus newly frozen water: 0.0997006 kg.

q.given: A small junction exchanges heat with a 100 °C source through an unknown resistance R_hot and with a 20 °C sink through an unknown R_cold. With no junction heater its steady temperature is 50 °C. Adding a 20.0 W heater at the junction raises its steady temperature to 60 °C. Resistances stay constant and there are no other heat paths. For a path, heat rate is temperature difference divided by resistance.
q.prompt: Infer R_hot, in K/W.
q.find: Infer R_hot, in K/W.
q.hint: Make a separate junction energy balance for each trial; the heater contributes power, not a temperature increment.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Without heating the two flows are both 37.5 W; with heating the full 30+20=50 W account closes.
q.feedback_incorrect: Adding 20 to a temperature is dimensionally wrong; add the heater to the power account.
q.explanation: Without the heater, (100−50)/R_hot=(50−20)/R_cold; hence R_cold=0.600R_hot. With 20.0 W added at the junction, (100−60)/R_hot+20.0=(60−20)/R_cold. Substitute the resistance ratio: 40/R_hot+20.0=66.6667/R_hot, giving 20.0R_hot=26.6667. Therefore R_hot=1.33333 K/W and R_cold=0.800 K/W. In the heater-on state, 30 W from the hot reservoir plus 20 W from the heater equals 50 W to the cold reservoir.

q.context: An insulated container receives 0.020 kg of steam at 100 °C, 0.10 kg of ice at −10 °C and 0.20 kg of water at 20 °C. Use L_v=2260, L_f=334 and c_water=4.2 in kJ-based units, and c_ice=2.1 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The container heat capacity is negligible and pressure is atmospheric. Explicitly, L_v=2260 kJ/kg, L_f=334 kJ/kg and c_water=4.2 kJ/(kg K). Assume no material leaves the container and mixing work is negligible.
q.prompt: Find the final equilibrium temperature.
q.hint: List each initial sample’s journey to the proposed common state, keeping sensible and latent stages separate.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. At the computed temperature both release and absorption totals are about 51.42 kJ; no initial ice or steam remains.
q.feedback_incorrect: Condensation does not finish the incoming steam’s journey: the condensed water must also cool to the final temperature.
q.explanation: Use kJ consistently. The steam can release 0.020×2260=45.2 kJ on condensation and then 0.020×4.2(100−T)=0.084(100−T) kJ on cooling. Initial ice needs 0.10×2.1×10=2.1 kJ to warm to 0 °C and 0.10×334=33.4 kJ to melt; its liquid then needs 0.42T kJ. The initial 0.20 kg water changes energy by 0.20×4.2(T−20)=0.84(T−20) kJ; this signed expression allows either cooling or warming. Set 45.2+0.084(100−T)=2.1+33.4+0.42T+0.84(T−20). Expanding gives 53.6−0.084T=18.7+1.26T. Hence 1.344T=34.9 and T=25.9673 °C, reported as 26.0 °C. The final temperature lies strictly between 0 and 100 °C at atmospheric pressure, consistent with the assumed all-liquid state.

q.prompt: Which measurement and interpretation provide the strongest valid discrimination among these choices?
q.find: Which measurement and interpretation provide the strongest valid discrimination among these choices?
q.hint: Compare both prediction separation and the model’s allowed range.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. A 15 W gap is much larger than the 4 W combined width of two ±2 W bands; the test remains below the 35 K limit.
q.feedback_incorrect: A larger extrapolated gap outside the valid range is not a valid discrimination test.
q.explanation: At 10 K rise, model A predicts 10 W and B predicts 0.050×10²=5 W: separation 5 W. At 30 K rise, the predictions are 30 W and 45 W: separation 15 W. At 40 K both models are outside the allowed range. Choose Option 2: measure at 30 K. A result agreeing with neither prediction would challenge both models rather than force a choice.

q.prompt: Find the steam mass percentage in each incoming packet.

q.feedback_incorrect: Assuming the cup capacity or averaging final temperatures discards one unknown rather than identifying it.
q.explanation: Let S be the latent heat released by each packet. Packet liquid cooling contributes 0.0200c(100−T_f); water plus cup receive(m_wc+C)(T_f−20). Run 1 gives S=6720+10C; run 2 gives S=8400+5C. Thus C=336 J/K and S=10080 J. Since S=0.0200xL, the steam fraction is x=10080/45200=0.223009, or 22.3009%.

q.context: A small spherical world receives a uniform parallel light flux S=1000 W/m². It reflects 30.0% of incoming light and absorbs the rest over its projected disk area πr². q.given: A small spherical world receives a uniform parallel light flux S=1000 W/m². It reflects 30.0% of incoming light and absorbs the rest over its projected disk area πr². It emits uniformly over its full area 4πr² with emissivity 0.90. Use emitted power εσAT⁴ with σ=5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m² K⁴). Ignore other heat flows and surrounding radiation.
q.prompt: Calculate its radiative equilibrium temperature, in K.
q.find: Calculate its radiative equilibrium temperature, in K.
q.hint: Identify the intercepting and emitting areas separately before making an energy balance.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Radius cancels because both areas scale as r². Using a disk area for emission would overestimate T by 4^(1/4).
q.feedback_incorrect: The 30% reflected fraction controls absorbed sunlight; ε=0.90 independently controls emitted infrared.
q.explanation: The absorbed fraction is 1−0.300=0.700. Incoming absorbed power is 0.700×1000×πr² W. Full-surface emitted power is 0.90×σ×4πr²×T⁴. At the stated radiative equilibrium set it equal to absorbed power. Cancel the common πr²: 700=4×0.90×5.67×10⁻⁸×T⁴. Take the positive fourth root: T=[700/(4×0.90×5.67×10⁻⁸)]^(1/4)=241.994 K.

q.given: A model leaf is kept at 20 °C in 30 °C air. Air-to-leaf heat transfer is k(T_air−T_leaf), with k=2.00 W/K. The leaf also absorbs 30.0 W of light. At steady temperature its only heat-removal mechanism is evaporation, with latent heat 2.40×10⁶ J/kg. Ignore metabolism, radiation exchange and changes in stored energy.
q.prompt: Find the mass of water that must evaporate each hour, in g.
q.find: Find the mass of water that must evaporate each hour, in g.
q.hint: Decide the sign of the air exchange from the temperatures, then identify the only outward energy pathway.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. 75.0 g/hour×(1 kg/1000 g)×2.40×10⁶ J/kg divided by 3600 s/hour gives 50.0 W.
q.feedback_incorrect: The cooler leaf receives energy from the warm air; treating that term as a loss underestimates evaporation.
q.explanation: Air-to-leaf transfer is k(T_air−T_leaf)=2.00×(30−20)=20.0 W into the leaf. Add absorbed light: total inward power is 20.0+30.0=50.0 W; evaporation must remove this at steady temperature. In one hour, evaporative energy is 50.0×3600=180000 J. The required evaporated mass is 180000/(2.40×10⁶)=0.0750 kg=75.0 g each hour.

q.context: Two wall panels have the same area and thickness and begin at 20 °C. Their outside surfaces are stepped to 60 °C. After two minutes the inner face of A is 25 °C and B is 30 °C. Their heat capacities are unknown and may differ. No steady heat-rate measurement has been made.
q.given: Two wall panels have the same area and thickness and begin at 20 °C. Their outside surfaces are stepped to 60 °C. After two minutes the inner face of A is 25 °C and B is 30 °C. Their heat capacities are unknown and may differ. No steady heat-rate measurement has been made.
q.prompt: Which conclusion and follow-up test are supported?
q.find: Which conclusion and follow-up test are supported?
q.hint: Ask whether the measurement includes an unknown rate of energy storage.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Equal thickness alone does not fix resistance: material conductivity and other paths matter.
q.feedback_incorrect: A slower initial temperature rise does not establish a universal steady insulation advantage.
q.explanation: During the first two minutes, input can increase panel internal energy as well as pass through the panel. A lower inner-face temperature could arise from greater energy storage, greater resistance or both; the unknown capacities allow competing explanations. Choose Option 3. Hold equal controlled boundary temperatures, wait for steady state and measure heat rate per area, controlling leakage and surface conditions. At steady state the storage term vanishes. With matched area and boundary ΔT, lower heat rate then indicates larger total thermal resistance in the tested configuration.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Transient temperature does not identify steady resistance
worked_solution.model: Before steady state a panel both stores and transmits energy. One transient temperature reading cannot determine both its capacity and its resistance.
steps: During the first two minutes, input can increase panel internal energy as well as pass through the panel.
A lower inner-face temperature could arise from greater energy storage, greater resistance or both; the unknown capacities allow competing explanations.
Choose Option 3. Hold equal controlled boundary temperatures, wait for steady state and measure heat rate per area, controlling leakage and surface conditions.
At steady state the storage term vanishes. With matched area and boundary ΔT, lower heat rate then indicates larger total thermal resistance in the tested configuration.
worked_solution.final_answer: Capacity and resistance are confounded; compare steady heat rates at the same area and boundary temperatures.
worked_solution.check: Equal thickness alone does not fix resistance: material conductivity and other paths matter.
worked_solution.common_error: A slower initial temperature rise does not establish a universal steady insulation advantage.

options: A necessarily has greater steady resistance; repeating the two-minute reading alone will identify it.
B necessarily has greater heat capacity; one transient reading separates capacity from resistance.
Capacity and resistance are confounded; compare steady heat rates at the same area and boundary temperatures.
Both panels must have the same steady resistance because their thicknesses match.

q.context: A string is replaced by one of the same material and length but twice the diameter. Its tension is then made nine times the original tension.
q.prompt: Find the final fundamental frequency as a multiple of the original frequency.
q.hint: Track the square of diameter in linear density.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The net factor is √(9/4)=1.50.
q.feedback_incorrect: Doubling diameter does not merely double cross-sectional area.
q.explanation: Same material and length make μ proportional to diameter squared; fundamental frequency scales with √(F_T/μ). Doubling diameter makes μ four times larger, reducing f by 2. Multiplying tension by 9 raises f by 3, so the net factor is 3/2=1.50.

q.context: Two displacement-amplitude resonance curves have the same measured peak frequency. B has a lower, broader peak. The drive amplitudes and masses are equal, but stiffnesses have not been measured.
q.given: Two displacement-amplitude resonance curves have the same measured peak frequency. B has a lower, broader peak. The drive amplitudes and masses are equal, but stiffnesses have not been measured.
q.prompt: Which conclusion is justified?
q.find: Which conclusion is justified?
q.hint: Separate driven peak position from undamped natural frequency.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. An independent stiffness or free-response measurement would add information absent from peak position alone.
q.feedback_incorrect: Equal forced peak frequencies do not prove equal undamped natural frequencies.
q.explanation: A broader lower displacement peak is consistent with stronger damping, while unknown stiffness prevents a unique natural-frequency comparison. Damping normally lowers and broadens a driven resonance peak. For a damped oscillator the displacement peak need not equal the undamped natural frequency. The observed curves support a damping explanation, while independent stiffness or free-oscillation measurements are needed to establish natural frequencies.

q.given: A stationary transmitter sends 500 Hz sound towards a wall approaching it at 20.0 m/s. Sound speed is 340 m/s in still air. For a moving receiver, the encounter frequency is f_r=f_s(v+u)/v when approaching; a moving source emits towards a stationary observer at f_o=f_r v/(v−u). Here reflection makes the wall first a receiver, then a source.
q.context: A stationary transmitter sends 500 Hz sound towards a wall approaching it at 20.0 m/s. Sound speed is 340 m/s in still air. Here reflection makes the wall first a receiver, then a source.
q.find: Find the reflected frequency measured at the transmitter.
q.prompt: Find the reflected frequency measured at the transmitter.
q.hint: Track what frequency is measured in each stage.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The complete ratio is 360/320=1.125, not either one-stage ratio.
q.feedback_incorrect: Applying only the moving-source formula misses the wall’s changed encounter rate.
q.explanation: The approaching wall encounters crests at 500(360/340)=529.412 Hz. Reflection preserves that encounter rate in the wall frame; the reflected crests then leave an approaching source. The transmitter measures 529.412(340/320)=562.5 Hz.

q.context: A string has fundamental 100 Hz. After an intervention it has 80 Hz. Two explanations are proposed: its tension fell to 64%, or its linear density rose to 156.25%. Length is unchanged.
q.given: A string has fundamental 100 Hz. After an intervention it has 80 Hz. Two explanations are proposed: its tension fell to 64%, or its linear density rose to 156.25%. Length is unchanged.
q.prompt: Which independent measurement distinguishes these two explanations?
q.find: Which independent measurement distinguishes these two explanations?
q.hint: Identify a measurement that responds differently to the hypotheses.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Both hypotheses give frequency factor 0.80; frequency repeats cannot separate them.
q.feedback_incorrect: Greater precision in the same dependent quantity does not create a new constraint.
q.explanation: All ideal harmonic frequencies depend on the same tension-to-density ratio, so a direct force measurement supplies independent evidence. For a uniform ideal string every harmonic scales with √(T/μ). Both proposed changes make T/μ equal to 64% of its original value, so every harmonic frequency scales identically. A direct tension measurement separates the hypotheses; more of the same frequency data do not.

q.feedback_correct: Correct. Doubling extension doubles tension, but L and μ also change; the final factor is √(5/3).
q.feedback_incorrect: Constant material volume does not imply constant linear density.
q.explanation: The supplied elastic tension follows extension, while fixed total mass makes μ inversely proportional to current length. Doubling extension from 0.200 to 0.400 m doubles tension. q.given: A tube model is f=v/[4(L+δ)] with unknown v and fixed end correction δ. Frequencies are 100 Hz at L=0.750 m and 80 Hz at L=0.950 m. A third measurement at L=1.150 m is 68.0±0.3 Hz. Treat the first two readings as exact calibration.
q.context: A tube model is f=v/[4(L+δ)] with unknown v and fixed end correction δ. Frequencies are 100 Hz at L=0.750 m and 80 Hz at L=0.950 m. A third measurement at L=1.150 m is 68.0±0.3 Hz. Treat the first two readings as exact calibration.
q.find: By how many hertz does the third central reading exceed the fitted prediction?
q.prompt: By how many hertz does the third central reading exceed the fitted prediction?
q.hint: Fit first, predict second, and compare the residual with its uncertainty.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Refitting the model to the third point would destroy its role as independent validation.
q.feedback_incorrect: A model that exactly fits two free parameters to two readings has not yet been independently tested.
q.explanation: The first two readings give 100(0.750+δ)=80(0.950+δ), henceδ=0.0500 m andv=320 m/s. The independent prediction is 320/[4(1.150+0.0500)]=66.6667 Hz. The excess is 68.0−66.6667=1.33333 Hz, greater than the stated 0.3 Hz half-width; the model fails this check.

q.given: A loudspeaker and microphone are at the same fixed point 2.00 m from a reflecting plane wall. Direct electrical reference timing is exact. Echoes of repeated pulses return 11.7647 ms after emission. A continuous tone gives successive destructive direct/echo interference frequencies 85.0 Hz apart. Assume one dominant reflection and constant sound speed. The lowest positive destructive frequency is 42.5 Hz.
q.context: A loudspeaker and microphone are at the same fixed point 2.00 m from a reflecting plane wall. Direct electrical reference timing is exact. Echoes of repeated pulses return 11.7647 ms after emission. A continuous tone gives successive destructive direct/echo interference frequencies 85.0 Hz apart. Assume one dominant reflection and constant sound speed. The lowest positive destructive frequency is 42.5 Hz.
q.find: Find the reflection phase reversal in degrees: enter 0 for no reversal or 180 for inversion.
q.prompt: Find the reflection phase reversal in degrees: enter 0 for no reversal or 180 for inversion.
q.hint: Separate phase information from frequency spacing.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. At 42.5 Hz, the propagation delay alone gives a half-cycle; no additional reversal is needed.
q.feedback_incorrect: Spacing determines delay but does not on its own determine a fixed reflection phase.
q.explanation: The round-trip path is 4.00 m and the echo gives speed 4/0.0117647≈340 m/s. For one fixed extra delayτ, successive cancellation frequencies are separated by 1/τ=85 Hz, consistent with the pulse result. At the lowest cancellation 42.5 Hz the propagation phase is 180°; the wall therefore adds no extra inversion.

q.given: A pulse in a uniform medium travels to a reflector and back. Received intensity follows I=C exp(−αs), where s is total path length; the pulse is confined to a uniform guide with negligible geometric spreading and C is constant. At reflector distances 0.200 m and 0.500 m the intensities are 64 and 16 units. A usable echo requires at least 4 units.
q.context: A pulse in a uniform medium travels to a reflector and back. q.find: Find the largest reflector distance giving a usable echo.
q.prompt: Find the largest reflector distance giving a usable echo.
q.hint: Calibrate attenuation with a ratio, then apply the detection boundary.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The return path doubles every added reflector distance; the unknown source factor cancels in ratios.
q.feedback_incorrect: Applying the attenuation exponent to one-way rather than total travel gives a wrong fitted absorption coefficient.

q.given: In a uniform guide/source arrangement the measured intensity is I=K(r/1m)^(−p) exp(−αr). Here K is a constant intensity scale, p is an unknown geometrical exponent and α is an unknown positive absorption coefficient in m⁻¹. Source output is constant. At distances 1.00,2.00,4.00 m, measured intensities are 8.00,1.00,0.0625 units. Treat the model as exact.
q.context: In a uniform guide/source arrangement the measured intensity is I=K(r/1m)^(−p) exp(−αr). Here K is a constant intensity scale, p is an unknown geometrical exponent and α is an unknown positive absorption coefficient in m⁻¹. Source output is constant. At distances 1.00,2.00,4.00 m, measured intensities are 8.00,1.00,0.0625 units. Treat the model as exact.
q.find: Find p.
q.prompt: Find p.
q.hint: Use equal distance ratios with unequal distance increments to remove the geometric exponent once.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. K=16 units reproduces all three readings; neither pure geometric loss nor pure absorption fits this inferred parameter pair.
q.feedback_incorrect: Attributing all measured intensity reduction to a single mechanism hides the other unknown parameter.
q.explanation: The first distance ratio gives 1/8=2^(−p)exp(−α×1m). The second gives 1/16=2^(−p)exp(−α×2m). Dividing eliminates p and gives exp(−α×1m)=1/2, so α=ln 2 m⁻¹. Then 2^(−p)=(1/8)/(1/2)=1/4, giving p=2. This inference separates two different attenuation mechanisms.

q.given: Two coherent equal-frequency sources give displacements a cosωt and b cos(ωt+φ) at a detector. For their resultant, intensity is proportional to a²+b²+2ab cosφ. Separately the sources give intensities 9 and 4 units. With both on, the intensity is 7 units. Ignore background. Here a and b are the arriving displacement amplitudes in a common unit, ω is their shared angular frequency in rad/s, t is time in s, and φ is their relative phase.
q.context: Two coherent equal-frequency sources give displacements a cosωt and b cos(ωt+φ) at a detector. For their resultant, intensity is proportional to a²+b²+2ab cosφ. Separately the sources give intensities 9 and 4 units. With both on, the intensity is 7 units. Ignore background. Here a and b are the arriving displacement amplitudes in a common unit, ω is their shared angular frequency in rad/s, t is time in s, and φ is their relative phase.
q.find: Find the smaller phase difference between their detector signals.
q.prompt: Find the smaller phase difference between their detector signals.
q.hint: Convert the separate intensity readings into amplitudes before inferring phase.
q.feedback_correct: The possible readout range is (√9−√4)²=1 to (√9+√4)²=25. Even at 180°, unequal arriving amplitudes leave 1 unit rather than zero; the measured 7 is consistent with 120°.
q.feedback_incorrect: Adding the two separate intensities without checking relative phase discards the coherent cross term.
q.explanation: The separate readings are I₁=9 and I₂=4. Their coherent cross-term coefficient is 2√(I₁I₂)=2√36=12 in the common intensity unit. The measured combined reading gives 7=9+4+12cosφ, so cosφ=−6/12=−0.500. The smaller phase angle is 120°. It is neither in-phase addition nor phase opposition; other phase angles differing by full cycles do not change the reading.

worked_solution.tested_idea: A two-source amplitude measurement must include propagation phase
worked_solution.model: Use the stated coherent-superposition response with one common calibration. Since each individual intensity is proportional to its squared displacement amplitude, the cross term can be written using the two measured individual intensities.

q.context: A laser passes through a wide doorway, while the same colour is later sent through a slit only a few wavelengths wide.
q.prompt: Which modelling choice is best?
options: Use rays for both because light always travels straight
Use the wave model for both because ray diagrams are never valid
Use rays for the doorway path and a wave model for the narrow slit
Use sound-wave equations for the slit
q.hint: Compare each opening with one wavelength.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The slit is only a few wavelengths wide, so spreading matters.
q.feedback_incorrect: Choosing a model depends on length scale, not on the colour alone.
q.explanation: Rays approximate large-scale paths; a wavelength-scale slit requires diffraction. q.given: A collimated 20.0 W beam crosses a slab whose two surfaces each transmit 90.0%. The emerging beam is 8.10 W. Ignore multiple internal reflections; bulk transmission is exp(−αx), and x=2.00 m is the actual ray path within the material.
q.prompt: Find α.
q.find: Find α.
q.hint: Remove both surface losses before inferring bulk loss.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. The bulk factor is exactly one half across 2 m.
q.feedback_incorrect: Using 8.10/20.0 directly incorrectly includes surface loss in α.
q.explanation: Surface transmission multiplies exponential bulk transmission. The power after surface losses alone would be 20.0×0.900²=16.2 W. The bulk transmission is 8.10/16.2=0.500=exp(−2.00α). α=ln2/2.00=0.346574 m⁻¹.

q.hint: Compare photon energies before total powers.

q.given: A small-angle diffraction experiment follows x=λD/a, with x the centre-to-first-minimum distance. The screen scale has a fixed additive offset z, so the recorded position is y=x+z. For one slit, y=3.40 mm at D=1.00 m and 5.80 mm at D=2.00 m. Wavelength is 600 nm.
q.context: A small-angle diffraction experiment follows x=λD/a, with x the centre-to-first-minimum distance. The screen scale has a fixed additive offset z, so the recorded position is y=x+z. For one slit, y=3.40 mm at D=1.00 m and 5.80 mm at D=2.00 m. Wavelength is 600 nm.
q.find: Find the slit width in millimetres.
q.prompt: Find the slit width in millimetres.
q.hint: Use a controlled distance change to eliminate the nuisance offset.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Both readings are reproduced by a 2.40 mm/m slope plus 1.00 mm offset.
q.feedback_incorrect: Dividing either uncorrected scale reading by distance treats a scale origin as a physical width.
q.explanation: Subtract readings: the true diffraction distance grows 2.40 mm for a 1.00 m screen shift. Thus λ/a=0.00240, independently of the scale offset. Slit width=600×10⁻⁹/0.00240=0.000250 m=0.250 mm; the offset is 1.00 mm.

q.given: A luminous line source of unknown width S and an opaque centred strip of width 0.0400 m are parallel. Source-to-strip separation a is unknown. A screen 0.100 m behind the strip shows a full-dark umbra of width 0.0200 m. The entire region dimmed by any amount, including penumbra, has width 0.0800 m. Neglect diffraction; all widths are measured in the source-width direction.
q.context: A luminous line source of unknown width S and an opaque centred strip of width 0.0400 m are parallel. Source-to-strip separation a is unknown. A screen 0.100 m behind the strip shows a full-dark umbra of width 0.0200 m. The entire region dimmed by any amount, including penumbra, has width 0.0800 m. Neglect diffraction; all widths are measured in the source-width direction.
q.find: Find a.
q.prompt: Find a.
q.hint: Construct the two sets of extreme rays and eliminate the unknown source width.
q.feedback_correct: Correct. Both observed widths are needed; the umbra alone would identify only a ratio.
q.feedback_incorrect: The full-dark overlap and the whole dimmed region have different extreme-ray boundaries.
q.explanation: Let w=0.0400 m be strip width, d=0.100 m strip-to-screen distance, U=0.0200 m umbra width and P=0.0800 m total dimmed width. S is source width and a is source-to-strip distance. On the screen, matching-edge rays give U=w−(S−w)d/a; opposite-edge rays give P=w+(S+w)d/a. Thus(S−w)/a=(0.0400−0.0200)/0.100=0.200 and(S+w)/a=(0.0800−0.0400)/0.100=0.400. Subtracting eliminates S:2w/a=0.200, so a=0.400 m. Then S=0.120 m checks both boundaries.

q.given: A bottom mark is viewed through a liquid of unknown depth d and a 0.0400 m glass cover of index 1.60. The cover touches the liquid; there is no air gap. Its near-normal apparent depth below the cover top is 0.2250 m. All interfaces are parallel. Air index is 1.00.

q.find: Find the liquid refractive index.
q.prompt: Find the liquid refractive index.
q.hint: Write an independent equation from each measurement.
q.feedback_correct: Back-substitution gives apparent depth 0.312616/1.56308+0.0400/1.60=0.2250 m and n sin i≈0.676189=1.60sin25°. Both independent observations agree.
q.feedback_incorrect: The glass cover affects apparent depth even though the ray data refer to its lower face.
q.explanation: Let n be the liquid refractive index and i its ray angle to the normal. In the near-normal observation, each layer contributes thickness/index: 0.2250=d/n+0.0400/1.60, so d/n=0.2000 m and d=(0.2000 m)n. In the separate oblique observation, the ray travels 0.1500 m horizontally while rising d. The right triangle gives sin i=0.1500/√(d²+0.1500²), with both lengths in m. Snell’s law at the liquid/glass boundary gives n sin i=1.60sin25.0°. Write k=1.60sin25.0°=0.676189 (dimensionless). Substitute d=0.2000n using m for lengths: 0.1500n/√(0.0400n²+0.02250)=k. Square and collect terms: 0.02250n²=k²(0.0400n²+0.02250), so n²=0.02250k²/(0.02250−0.0400k²)=2.44322. Select the positive physical index n=1.56308. Then d=0.312616 m. The liquid angle is arctan(0.1500/0.312616)=25.633°; the given glass angle is 25.0°. The near-normal approximation applies to the depth observation, not to this oblique ray.
